title: DCS — Discite Computatrum Scientia
subtitle: Computer science education that doesn't need a computer.

sections.heading: Current Status
sections.content:
The course is written and reviewed, and the storytelling has begun. All 18 lessons of the DCS Programming Course are complete — 54 documents in all: a lesson plan, a teacher guide, and a student handout for each one. Every lesson now opens with a story from the Farmer Joe universe, a wacky farm where the computer science hides inside the plot.

Who's on the farm: Farmer Joe, who does exactly what he is told — nothing more, nothing less. Mrs Joe, who does not like the sun and sends her instructions on a note through the kitchen window. The cat — nonchalant, thoroughly spoilt, and quite certain it knows best (it usually doesn't). The cow — so literal that doing exactly as she is told is what gets everyone into trouble. And the monkeys, enthusiastic helpers who simply cannot resist one more row.

The canon map behind those stories went through an independent correctness review — zero wrong computer science found, and every fix folded in. Next up are the standalone concept-stories learners can retell at home, teacher training, and the first mechanical computing devices.
items: 18 lessons complete — a plan, a teacher guide, and a student handout for each
Story-first: every concept lives in the Farmer Joe universe, and the technical term arrives as the punchline
Canon map independently reviewed — zero wrong CS found, fixes applied and approved
Next: the story series, teacher training, and the first mechanical devices

sections.heading: The Why
sections.content:
Millions of children in rural communities will never touch a computer in a classroom. But the thinking behind computer science — breaking a problem into pieces, spotting patterns, setting aside what doesn't matter, putting steps in the right order — doesn't need a screen.

It needs a teacher who knows how to play the right games. So DCS is a curriculum built from things a classroom already has: board games, card games, group challenges, stories, and a lot of moving about. The children count with stones, carry water with bottle caps, argue about instructions, and laugh when the instructions are wrong. The ideas stick because they were never abstract in the first place.

These learners are not being prepared to survive the digital world as passive consumers. They are being prepared to shape it.

sections.heading: The Vision
sections.content:
Years ago I wrote that every child should learn computer science — not to become a programmer, but to become a creator. Someone who understands the logic behind the tools they use, instead of simply consuming whatever technology hands them. That idea has not aged a day.

DCS is that idea made practical: a full lesson series built for the reality of rural classrooms, where a teacher's imagination matters far more than a computer lab budget. It was revived in 2026 with a sharper shape — two pillars, computational thinking and programming as a way of thinking, for learners from middle school upward.

The world these children are growing into is more digital every year. The point is that they walk into it as the people who build things, not the people things are built for.

sections.heading: What's Next
sections.content:
The skeleton of the course is finished, so now it gets its stories. The Farmer Joe universe grows into a standalone series: warm, funny stories that carry the ideas and go home with the children — the kind a child retells at lunch, and still remembers years later.

After that comes teacher training, so a teacher with no technology background can walk into a room and run a full lesson with chalk, stones, and bottle caps. And further out, a small collection of mechanical computers from history — the abacus, the slide rule, stepped drums. Buildable, affordable, and not a single battery between them.
items: The story series — standalone Farmer Joe stories, one per concept
Teacher training — one teacher, several grades in one room
Mechanical computing devices — abacus, slide rule, stepped drums
Materials stay village-sourced: chalk, stones, bottle caps, string, paper
